tldr: By applying counterfactual action augmentation (SIDO) to static object teleoperation data to preserve hand-object relative poses, this work enables policies to accurately grasp and manipulate moving objects at test time—without ever seeing moving objects during training.
hero_caption: Overview of SIDO. During training, object positions from static demonstrations are counterfactually displaced, and action chunks are morphed to maintain hand-object relative poses, learning a goal-conditioned policy. At deployment, an object pose predictor supplies future positions to adapt to moving objects.
overview:
Visuomotor policies trained with imitation learning have achieved impressive progress. However, most rely on the implicit assumption that target objects stay static while the robot executes its task. In the real world, parts drift on conveyors and fruits sway in the wind. Collecting new teleoperation data on such moving objects is extremely costly, dangerous, and overfits to the specific motions seen during data collection.

The authors recognized that moving object manipulation factorizes into two sub-problems: predicting where the object will be in the future, and reaching that predicted future pose while maintaining the proper hand-object relative pose. Because static demonstrations already contain rich reach-and-grasp behaviors for the latter, the authors developed Static In, Dynamic Out (SIDO). SIDO is a counterfactual action augmentation method that displaces the object position and morphs demonstrated hand trajectories to preserve relative poses.

Evaluated on three simulated tasks across five motion patterns and two real-world tasks (Gantry and Peachtree), SIDO significantly improved grasping success on moving objects over baselines without degrading static object performance. This demonstrates that dynamic manipulation tasks can be solved without collecting new real-world dynamic demonstrations, simply by combining geometric prior-based data augmentation with future pose predictors.
contributions: Proposed a modular, factorized framework that separates moving object manipulation into object motion prediction and relative-pose-preserving reaching to that predicted pose.

Developed counterfactual action augmentation techniques (a heuristic variant, H-SIDO, and a robot dynamics-aware variant, DynaSIDO) that preserve hand-object relative pose invariance from static demonstrations.
Established a framework where motion predictors can be swapped plug-and-play at test time without any policy retraining.
Demonstrated significant improvements in manipulation success on unseen object motions across simulation and two real-world platforms, all while preserving static performance.

sections.heading: Can a robot grasp moving objects using only static data?
sections.summary: Most robot imitation learning assumes static targets, but objects move frequently in the real world. SIDO avoids costly dynamic data collection by counterfactually augmenting static demonstrations to manipulate moving objects.
sections.details:
Behavior Cloning (BC) using diffusion models and Transformers has advanced significantly, but its success relies on training data covering deployment conditions. Real deployments frequently violate the static assumption: parts drift on conveyors and fruits sway in the wind. Collecting teleoperation demonstrations on moving objects is difficult, hazardous, and biases the policy toward the specific motions observed during collection.

The key insight is that moving object manipulation naturally factorizes into two independent sub-problems:
- (1) A position prediction problem: guessing where the object will be over the action chunk horizon (learnable purely from trajectory tracking without teleoperation).
- (2) A goal-conditioned reaching problem: generating actions that achieve the correct hand-object relative pose relative to that predicted pose (already richly present in static demos).

SIDO decouples these two components. During training, it counterfactually shifts object positions in static demonstrations and morphs action chunks to maintain relative poses, training a goal-conditioned policy. At test time, any off-the-shelf object pose predictor can be connected in a plug-and-play manner.

sections.heading: How does this differ from reactive policies and data augmentation?
sections.summary: Reactive policies, equivariant policies, and conventional counterfactual augmentations do not directly account for temporal displacements of objects. SIDO is unique in explicitly injecting geometric and temporal counterfactuals directly into the training data.
sections.details:
The distinctions from prior work can be categorized into three main areas:

Imitation Learning and Covariate Shift:
To counter covariate shift caused by cascading action errors, researchers have developed reactive policies with minimal latency or collected large volumes of dynamic demonstrations (e.g., PUMA). However, reactive policies still assume the training distribution covers target motions, while collecting dynamic demonstrations incurs massive operational costs. SIDO embeds future displacements directly into training data by morphing static demonstrations.

Object Pose Prediction:
Techniques combining 6D pose estimators like FoundationPose with classical filters or neural predictors like FERNN are mature. Because SIDO cleanly isolates the policy from the predictor, one can swap in the best-performing predictor without retraining the policy.

Data Augmentation and Structural Priors:
Spatial and semantic counterfactual relabeling and equivariance-based models exploit spatial symmetries, but they do not handle temporal displacement from object motion. SIDO explicitly injects geometric and temporal priors by preserving hand-object relative poses across the action chunk.

sections.heading: Why policies trained on static data fail on moving targets
sections.summary: Behavior cloning fails on moving objects because of a vicious cycle: action mismatch from ignoring future motion during execution, followed by out-of-distribution visual drift after missing the target.
sections.details:
Consider a setup where a policy $\pi_\theta$ receives robot proprioception $s_t$, camera images, and 3D object position $P_t$, then predicts an action chunk of $T_p$ steps, executing the first $T_a$ steps before replanning.

In static training demonstrations, the pre-grasp object position is always a constant $P_{\text{static}}$. In deployment, however, the object moves along an unknown trajectory $\xi(t)$. This causes two cascading failures:
- Action mismatch: Because the target continues moving during execution, actions decided at time $t$ must reach where the object will be at $\xi(t+T_p)$, rather than its current position $\xi(t)$. Static demonstrations lack these anticipatory actions.
- Out-of-distribution observation: The gripper targets an outdated past position and misses. As a result, observations—such as wrist-camera views—diverge sharply from the training distribution.

sections.heading: The core of SIDO: morphing action chunks while preserving relative poses
sections.summary: Static demonstrations are counterfactually shifted, and action chunks are morphed to maintain hand-object relative poses. Two approaches are proposed: a simple linear ramp (H-SIDO) and an optimization scheme using a dynamics model (DynaSIDO).
sections.details:
At the heart of the method is the hand-object relative pose Invariant Constraint. Defining the offset between end-effector pose $p_t^{\text{eef}}$ and object pose $P_t$ as $r_t(k) = p_{t+k}^{\text{eef}} - P_{t+k}$, the goal is to preserve $r_t(T_a)$ at the replanning step and $r_t(T_p)$ at the horizon, even as the object moves.

Counterfactual Augmentation Procedure:
A displacement $\delta = v T_p [\cos\theta, \sin\theta, 0]^\top$ is sampled along a random angle $\theta$ to define the counterfactual future position $\tilde{P}_{t+T_p} = P_{\text{static}} + \delta$. To retain static manipulation ability, a zero displacement is assigned with probability $\alpha$. The images remain untouched; only the object position channel is updated to $\tilde{P}_{t+T_p}$.

Two Action Morphing Approaches:
- H-SIDO (Heuristic): The displacement $\delta$ is distributed across the chunk via a linear ramp function $\rho_k$, shifting waypoints directly. For relative action representations, the ramp is applied along the trajectory arc length to preserve trajectory shape.
- DynaSIDO (Dynamics-aware): Because H-SIDO modifies command waypoints without accounting for tracking lag in real robot controllers, execution errors can occur. DynaSIDO learns a robot residual dynamics model $f_\psi$ from demonstration data and uses MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) control to optimize an action chunk that accurately reaches the targets at $T_a$ and $T_p$ under model predictions.

At deployment, the system operates simply by feeding the predicted future position $\hat{P}_{t+T_p}$ from an object pose predictor into the observation channel.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-world results: tracking performance and plug-and-play predictors
sections.summary: SIDO was evaluated against baselines across three simulated and two real-world tasks. It substantially boosted dynamic success rates while preserving static performance, confirming seamless predictor swappability.
sections.details:
Experiments used Diffusion Policy (DP) and Equivariant Diffusion Policy (EquiDP) as backbones to evaluate three core hypotheses:

Hypothesis 1: Can SIDO improve moving object success while preserving static performance?
Evaluated across simulation (Mug, Square, Stack at 2 cm/s) and real hardware (Gantry, Peachtree at 1.5 cm/s). On the real Gantry task under X-axis motion, standard DP achieved a 0.10 success rate and DP with current pose achieved 0.35, whereas DP+SIDO achieved 0.55. On Peachtree, performance increased from 0.45 (baseline) to 0.60. Under static conditions, SIDO matched or exceeded baselines, reaching 1.00 success.

Hypothesis 2: Is the hand-object relative pose maintained at the end of the action?
On the real Gantry, measuring the tracking slope $\beta_x$ of commanded end-effector position against object position showed DP+SIDO achieved 0.42 (closest to the expert reference of 0.62), outperforming DP (0.31) and DP cur. pose (0.10). t-SNE visualizations of wrist-camera features confirmed that DP+SIDO observations stayed within the static training distribution, avoiding miss-induced drift.

Hypothesis 3: Can policies and predictors be swapped flexibly?
SIDO delivered consistent gains on both DP and EquiDP. Furthermore, evaluating a fixed policy across finite difference, MLP, and FERNN predictors showed that FERNN—which achieved the lowest Final Displacement Error (FDE)—yielded the highest success rate (0.40), confirming modular plug-and-play compatibility.

sections.heading: Conclusions and limitations: bridging static data to dynamic worlds
sections.summary: SIDO enables dynamic object manipulation from static demonstrations via geometric prior-based data augmentation. Remaining challenges include reliance on external pose estimators and obstacle avoidance.
sections.details:
In conclusion, the temporal variability required for dynamic targets can be effectively bridged using explicit geometric priors (relative pose invariance) during training, demonstrating that static demonstrations provide a solid foundation for dynamic manipulation.

Current limitations include:
- Reliance on external pose estimators: The real-world system relies on FoundationPose, which requires CAD models or pre-scans for novel objects (though improvements in pose estimation directly enhance this framework).
- Obstacle collisions: The method does not explicitly consider obstacle collisions along shifted reaching paths, requiring future integration with collision-avoidance planners in cluttered environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: dynamic teleoperation comparisons and DynaSIDO at higher speeds
sections.summary: The appendix provides detailed analyses comparing SIDO to collecting dynamic teleoperation demonstrations, validating DynaSIDO under higher speeds, and assessing adaptability to speed variations.
sections.details:
The appendix presents several critical practical evaluations:

Dynamic Demonstration Collection vs. SIDO (Appendix B):
Policies trained on teleoperated demonstrations of moving objects were evaluated. Collecting dynamic demonstrations proved difficult: human teleoperation success dropped from 98.5% (static) to 59.8%, while collection time grew from 1h 49m to 2h 33m. Furthermore, because operators focused heavily on tracking, workspace coverage shrank to 80.02% of the static grid. Consequently, the dynamic-demonstration baseline achieved only a 0.05 success rate, whereas cheap static data combined with SIDO achieved 0.25.

Speed Scaling with H-SIDO vs. DynaSIDO (Appendix A):
At low speed (2 cm/s), H-SIDO and DynaSIDO achieved identical success rates (0.90). However, at 6 cm/s, H-SIDO's tracking degraded sharply to 0.05, while DynaSIDO maintained a 0.25 success rate by correcting the trajectory using the learned dynamics model, proving valuable in high-speed regimes.

Adaptation to Speed Variations (Appendix C):
By sampling displacement magnitudes across a continuous range during augmentation and pairing the policy with a FERNN predictor, SIDO sustained a 0.40 success rate even when object speeds varied dynamically between 1.5 and 4.5 cm/s at runtime.

captions.F7: Comparison of workspace coverage between static and dynamic demonstrations. Due to the high difficulty of teleoperating moving objects, dynamic demos only cover 80.02% of the workspace compared to the uniform grid coverage of static demos.

takeaways: Rather than solving moving object manipulation end-to-end, factorizing the task into future position prediction and relative-pose-preserving reaching is an effective design strategy.
Because teleoperating moving objects is costly and limits workspace coverage, counterfactually augmenting high-quality static demonstrations geometrically yields superior robustness.
While simple heuristic ramping (H-SIDO) works well at low speeds, compensating for robot tracking delays with a learned dynamics model (DynaSIDO) is crucial at higher velocities.
limitations: Depends on off-the-shelf 6D object pose estimators like FoundationPose, making immediate deployment challenging for novel objects without CAD models or prior 3D scans.
Because action chunks are shifted translationally, collision and interference avoidance in cluttered environments containing obstacles along the path is not addressed.
Current real-world experiments are limited to relatively modest speeds around 1.5 cm/s; real-world validation under faster object motions remains future work.
